analysis.one_liner: Shields waste generators and transporters from Superfund cleanup liability and blocks cost-sharing lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The Superfund liability moratorium died in House subcommittees without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Superfund law, anyone connected to a contaminated site can be made to pay for the cleanup, including companies that merely sent waste to a dump someone else ran. This bill would bar the EPA from pursuing cleanup enforcement against companies that did not directly cause a release and did not know about it, and would suspend the right of any party to sue other responsible parties to share cleanup costs, including lawsuits already pending in court. The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that generated hazardous waste or shipped it to disposal sites they did not own, and transporters who hauled it there, would be shielded from EPA cleanup enforcement. Parties already sued for cost contribution by others would also get relief while the moratorium lasted.

how_it_helps.text: Bars the EPA from continuing or starting enforcement actions against parties who arranged for disposal or transport of hazardous waste by others, so long as they did not directly cause the release and had no knowledge of it [S2] [S3].
Suspends the authority to seek contribution from other potentially liable parties during and after civil actions, including judicial actions already pending when the bill would take effect [S2] [S3].
Tolls limitation periods for cost-recovery and damage actions for the duration of the moratorium, so claims that would otherwise expire stay alive [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Superfund trust, financed by taxpayers, and any remaining responsible parties would absorb cleanup costs that shielded companies would otherwise bear. Parties that had already paid settlements could no longer recover shares from others. Communities near contaminated sites could face slower or less fully funded cleanups.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement moratorium would shift cleanup costs away from the companies that sent waste to a site and onto the Superfund trust, which is funded by taxpayers, and onto the parties left liable [S2] [S3].

The contribution moratorium would apply retroactively to lawsuits already pending in court, upending settled expectations for parties that had resolved their liability to the government and could no longer recover from others [S2] [S3].

A blanket suspension rather than a tailored reform would sweep in large firms alongside the small businesses and municipalities that Superfund liability critics most often cited, and would leave the question unresolved after the moratorium expired.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill responds to a real and widely acknowledged problem: parties with little connection to a site's contamination, such as small businesses and waste shippers, have been swept into Superfund liability. But this bill's remedy is a blanket, retroactive moratorium rather than a targeted reform, and its main effect would be to move cleanup costs from companies to the public trust and to the parties who remain on the hook. A more carefully drawn liability exemption would have addressed the same complaint at less cost to the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, and neither ever scheduled a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Canady introduced the bill on February 2, 1995, and it was referred to the House Commerce Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee [S1] [S5].
Within weeks it was sent to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment and the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade, and Hazardous Materials [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the 104th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, cleanup liability stayed with the companies that generated and hauled the waste, and taxpayers did not absorb those costs. Parties pursuing pending contribution claims also kept their day in court.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers and communities near waste sites

industries.industry: Hazardous waste generators and transporters (chemical, manufacturing, and shipping companies)
industries.note: The bill would exempt companies that sent waste to sites they did not own, and the haulers who moved it, from EPA cleanup enforcement, shifting those cleanup costs to the Superfund trust financed by taxpayers and to remaining liable parties.

industries.industry: Superfund settlement payers and contribution plaintiffs
industries.note: The moratorium on contribution actions would stop parties from suing each other to share cleanup costs, which relieves some defendants but also cuts off recovery for parties that had already paid more than their share, including in lawsuits already in court.
Suspending enforcement would reduce the cleanup actions that drive demand for remediation work, an indirect effect on the industry that performs Superfund cleanups.
